body_markdown:
Getting children back into a regular sleep schedule after the summer holidays can be challenging. Late nights, relaxed mealtimes and busy holiday routines can make the transition to early school mornings feel difficult for both children and parents.


While there is no single food that can instantly fix a child's sleep routine, nutrition may play a supporting role. A balanced diet provides important nutrients involved in normal body functions, including processes associated with sleep and relaxation.


According to nutritionist, three dietary areas are worth including in a child's everyday meals: milk, foods containing magnesium and foods that naturally contain melatonin. The advice is not about creating a special bedtime menu. Instead, the focus is on building nutritious foods into a child's normal routine.


## 1. Milk Can Be a Simple Addition to the Evening Routine


Milk is one of the easiest foods to include in a child's diet and may be a useful option as part of a relaxing evening routine.


Milk contains tryptophan, an amino acid that the body uses to produce serotonin and melatonin. Melatonin is a hormone involved in regulating the body's sleep-wake cycle. Some evidence also suggests that milky drinks may be associated with better sleep quality in both children and adults.


For parents looking for a straightforward option, a glass of milk can therefore be included as part of a balanced evening routine, provided the child normally tolerates dairy.


However, it is important not to confuse milk with sweetened chocolate drinks. Hot chocolate may contain caffeine, depending on the ingredients used, and caffeine can interfere with sleep. Parents should check labels and consider choosing caffeine-free options if a warm drink is being offered close to bedtime.


Milk is also a useful source of several nutrients, so it can contribute to an overall varied diet rather than being treated as a specific sleep remedy.


## 2. Magnesium-Rich Foods Support Everyday Nutrition


Magnesium is an essential mineral involved in numerous processes throughout the body. It contributes to normal muscle and nerve function and is also associated with processes involved in relaxation and sleep.


The good news is that children do not need to rely on supplements to get magnesium. A variety of everyday foods can provide it naturally.


Dark green vegetables such as spinach and kale are useful choices. Nuts and seeds can also contribute magnesium, while foods such as chickpeas and lentils provide another option.


Wholegrains are particularly easy to incorporate into family meals. Oats, wholemeal bread and brown rice are among the foods highlighted as magnesium sources. Dairy products and oily fish can also form part of a varied diet.


Rather than concentrating on giving children magnesium at a particular time of day, the nutrition advice suggests making these foods part of their regular meals.


For example, breakfast could include porridge made with milk and topped with fruit. Lunch might contain wholemeal bread alongside vegetables and a protein source. Dinner could include brown rice, vegetables and oily fish or legumes.


The goal is consistency rather than perfection.


## 3. Melatonin-Rich Foods Can Add Variety to Meals


Some foods naturally contain melatonin and can be included in a child's balanced diet. Examples mentioned by the nutritionist include tart cherries, goji berries, kiwi, eggs, cheese, oily fish and nuts such as almonds, walnuts and pistachios.


These foods offer parents plenty of choices without requiring a complicated meal plan.


Kiwi, for example, can be served as a snack or added to breakfast. Eggs can be incorporated into breakfast or lunch, while nuts can be included where they are age-appropriate and safe for the child. Oily fish can be served as part of a family dinner.


Importantly, there is limited evidence about exactly when these foods should be eaten to produce a sleep benefit. This means parents do not need to create a strict schedule around them.


Instead, incorporating a variety of nutritious foods throughout the day is a more practical approach.


## A Balanced Diet Matters More Than One "Sleep Food"


It can be tempting to search for one food that will solve a child's sleep problems. However, nutrition is only one part of healthy sleep.


The advice from Ruckledge emphasises looking at the overall diet rather than focusing too heavily on individual foods. A varied diet containing colourful plant-based foods, alongside appropriate dairy products, wholegrains and oily fish, can help children obtain a broad range of nutrients.


One simple approach is to encourage children to "eat a rainbow" by offering different coloured fruits and vegetables across the week. This can make meals more appealing while increasing dietary variety.


Parents also do not need to force children to eat foods they dislike simply because they have been associated with sleep. A child does not need to eat kale, fish or cheese immediately before bed to benefit from a nutritious diet.


Instead, these foods can be introduced naturally across breakfast, lunch, snacks and dinner.


## Getting Back Into a School Sleep Routine


Food can support healthy habits, but restoring a consistent routine is likely to involve more than diet alone.


After several weeks of holiday freedom, children may need time to adjust to earlier bedtimes and morning wake-ups. Gradually returning to regular meal and sleep times can make the change easier.


Creating a calm evening routine may also help. Parents can consider reducing stimulating activities before bedtime and keeping the bedroom environment comfortable and consistent.


For school-aged children, getting enough sleep is particularly important because inadequate sleep can affect daytime alertness, concentration, memory and general functioning.


According to the information cited in the source article, children aged six to 12 generally need around nine to 11 hours of sleep each night.


## The Takeaway for Parents


There is no magic food that can instantly reset a child's body clock. However, nutrition can form part of a wider healthy sleep routine.


Milk, magnesium-containing foods and foods that naturally contain melatonin are three dietary categories that parents can consider when planning balanced meals. Options include milk, leafy green vegetables, oats, wholemeal bread, brown rice, nuts, seeds, legumes, eggs, kiwi, tart cherries and oily fish.


The most useful strategy is not to focus on one particular "sleep food". Instead, aim for variety, regular meals and a balanced diet that provides children with the nutrients they need as they return to school.


A healthy evening routine, consistent sleep schedule and nutritious meals can work together to make the transition from summer holidays to school mornings smoother.


### Source


*The Sun* on 31 August 2026.


### Health Disclaimer


This article is intended for general information and educational purposes only. It does not constitute medical, nutritional or professional healthcare advice. Food cannot be relied upon as a treatment for persistent sleep problems. If a child regularly struggles to sleep, is excessively tired during the day or has ongoing concerns about their sleep, parents or carers should speak with a qualified healthcare professional. Parents should also consider a child's individual dietary requirements, allergies and age when introducing foods.
